title: Sea Stars of the Shore
summary: How sea stars, which are not really fish, move on tube feet, eat clams with their stomachs, regrow lost arms, and survive the tides on rocky shores.
poll: Sea stars are among the most amazing animals in the ocean.

versions.title: Sea Stars on the Shore
versions.text:
Look in a pool by the sea. You may see a sea star. Some call it a starfish. But it is not a fish at all!

Most sea stars have five arms. Some have more. A sea star has no brain. It has no blood. Sea water moves through its body.

Turn a sea star over. Look at its arms. You will see lots of tube feet. Each foot can grip like a cup. The feet help it creep on rocks. It moves quite slow.

Each arm has an eye spot at the tip. The spot can tell light from dark.

Sea stars like to eat clams. A sea star pulls the shell a bit open. Then it pushes its stomach out of its mouth. The stomach goes in the shell! It eats the clam there.

A sea star can lose an arm. Then it can regrow it. This takes a long time.

The tide goes out two times a day. Then sea stars stay in wet pools on the shore. Sea stars live in the Red Sea, too. If you see one, just look. Do not take it home.

A sea star can lose an arm. But it can regrow a new one. This can take many months.

The tide goes out two times every day. Then sea stars wait in wet pools on the shore. Sea stars live in the Red Sea, too. If you find one, just look. Leave it in its home.

Most sea stars have five arms. Some kinds have many more. A sea star has no brain and no blood. Instead, ocean water moves through its body.

Turn a sea star over gently. Under every arm are lots of tiny tube feet. Each foot can grip like a little cup. The feet help the sea star creep over rocks. It moves very slowly.

At the tip of each arm is a tiny eye spot. It cannot see shapes, but it can tell light from darkness.

If a sea star loses an arm, it can regrow a new one. This can take many months.

The tide goes out two times every day. Then sea stars stay in wet pools on the shore. Sea stars also live in the Red Sea near Saudi Arabia. If you find one, just look. Please leave it in its home.

versions.title: Sea Stars of the Shore
versions.text:
Walk along a rocky shore when the water is low, and look into the little pools of ocean water. You may spot a sea star clinging to a rock. Many people call it a starfish, but it is not a fish at all. It has no bones, no fins, and no gills like a fish.

Most sea stars have five arms that spread out from the middle. Some kinds have many more. A sea star has no brain and no blood. Instead, it pumps ocean water through its body.

If you turn a sea star over gently, you will notice rows of tiny tube feet under each arm. Each foot can grip like a little suction cup. Together, the feet help the sea star creep over rocks very slowly.

At the tip of each arm is a tiny eye spot. It cannot see clear shapes, but it can tell light from darkness.

Sea stars hunt clams and mussels. A sea star wraps its arms around a shell and pulls until the shell opens just a little. Then it pushes its stomach out of its mouth and into the shell! The stomach eats the soft animal inside.

If a sea star loses an arm, it can regrow a new one. This can take many months, or even a year.

The tide goes out two times every day. When it does, sea stars stay in wet pools on the shore. Sea stars also live in the Red Sea near Saudi Arabia. If you discover one, look closely, but leave it in its home.

versions.title: Sea Stars of the Shore
versions.text:
When the tide is low on a rocky shore, small pools of ocean water are left behind among the rocks. Look closely into one of these tide pools, and you may notice a sea star holding tightly to a stone. Many people call it a starfish, but it is not a fish at all. It has no backbone, no fins, and no gills like a fish. Its closest relatives are sea urchins and sand dollars. Together, these animals are called echinoderms.

Most sea stars have five arms that spread out from a center disk, although some kinds have twenty or more. A sea star has no brain and no blood. Instead, it pumps ocean water through a system of tubes inside its body.

Under each arm are hundreds of tiny tube feet. The water inside the tubes moves the feet, and each foot works like a small suction cup. Together, the feet let the sea star grip rocks and travel very slowly.

At the tip of each arm is a simple eye spot. It cannot see clear pictures, but it can sense light and darkness.

Sea stars are predators. They hunt clams, mussels, and snails. A sea star wraps its arms around a clam and pulls with its tube feet until the shell opens a tiny crack. Then it pushes its stomach out through its mouth and into the shell. The stomach starts to digest the clam right there.

If a sea star loses an arm to a hungry bird or crab, it can regrow a new one. This can take many months, or even a year.

Twice every day, the tide goes out. Then sea stars rest in tide pools or under damp seaweed until the water returns. Sea stars also live in the Red Sea near Saudi Arabia. One kind there, the crown-of-thorns sea star, eats coral. If you discover a sea star, observe it closely, but leave it in its home.

versions.title: Sea Stars of the Shore
versions.text:
Whenever the tide retreats from a rocky coastline, shallow pools of seawater remain trapped among the boulders. Anyone who carefully examines these tide pools may discover a sea star attached firmly to a rock. Although many people call this creature a starfish, it is not actually a fish, because it lacks a backbone, fins, and gills. It is an invertebrate, and its closest relatives are sea urchins and sand dollars, which scientists classify alongside it as echinoderms.

Most species possess five arms radiating from a central disk, although certain varieties have twenty or more. Remarkably, the animal has neither a brain nor blood. Instead, it circulates seawater through a network of internal canals called a water vascular system.

Underneath every arm are hundreds of miniature tube feet. Water pressure within the canals extends and retracts these feet, and each one operates like a tiny suction cup. Working cooperatively, they allow the echinoderm to grip rocks securely and to travel at a very gradual pace.

Positioned at the tip of every arm is a simple eye spot. Although it cannot produce detailed images, it can detect light and darkness, which helps the animal locate shadows and potential shelter.

Sea stars are skillful predators of clams, mussels, and snails. The hunter wraps its arms around a clam and pulls steadily with its tube feet until the tired muscles of its victim allow the shell to open slightly. It then pushes its stomach through its mouth and into the narrow opening, where it begins to digest the soft animal.

If a sea star loses an arm to a hungry seabird or crab, it can regenerate a replacement. This remarkable process may require several months, or even an entire year.

Twice every day the tide recedes. During this period, sea stars shelter in tide pools or underneath damp seaweed until the water returns. These animals also inhabit the Red Sea along the coastline of Saudi Arabia, where one species, the crown-of-thorns sea star, devours living coral. Because sea stars control the populations of many other animals, they play an important role in their ecosystem. Visitors who encounter one should observe it carefully but leave it undisturbed in its natural environment.

versions.title: Sea Stars of the Shore
versions.text:
Whenever the tide retreats from a rocky coastline, shallow pools of seawater remain trapped among the boulders. Anyone who carefully examines these temporary habitats may discover a sea star attached firmly to a rock. Although many people describe this creature as a starfish, it is not actually a fish, because it lacks a backbone, fins, and gills. It is an invertebrate, and its closest relatives are sea urchins and sand dollars, which scientists classify alongside it as echinoderms, a name meaning spiny skin.

Most species possess five arms radiating from a central disk, although certain varieties develop twenty or more. Remarkably, the animal has neither a brain nor blood. Instead, it circulates seawater through a network of internal canals, collectively identified as a water vascular system.

Underneath every arm are hundreds of miniature tube feet. Hydraulic pressure within the canals extends and retracts these appendages, and each one operates like a tiny suction cup. Functioning cooperatively, they enable the echinoderm to grip rocks securely and to travel at an extremely gradual pace.

Positioned at the tip of every arm is a primitive eye spot. Although it cannot produce detailed images, it can distinguish illumination from darkness, which helps the animal identify shadows and potential shelter.

Sea stars are formidable predators of clams, mussels, and snails. The hunter wraps its arms around a clam and pulls persistently with its tube feet until the exhausted muscles of its victim allow the shell to separate slightly. It then extends its stomach through its mouth and into the narrow opening, where digestion of the soft animal begins.

If a sea star loses an arm to a hungry seabird or crab, it can regenerate a replacement, although this remarkable process may require several months, or even an entire year.

Twice every day the tide recedes. During this period, sea stars shelter in tide pools or underneath damp seaweed until the returning water covers them again. These animals also inhabit the Red Sea along the coastline of Saudi Arabia, where one particular species, the crown-of-thorns sea star, devours living coral. Because sea stars regulate the populations of numerous other animals, they occupy an important position within their ecosystem. Consequently, visitors who encounter one should observe it attentively but leave it undisturbed in its natural environment.

versions.title: Sea Stars of the Shore
versions.text:
Whenever the tide retreats from a rocky coastline, shallow pools of seawater remain trapped among the boulders. Anyone who carefully examines these temporary habitats may discover a sea star attached tenaciously to a submerged surface. Although many people describe this creature as a starfish, it is not genuinely a fish, because it entirely lacks a backbone, fins, and gills. It is, in fact, an invertebrate whose closest relatives, the sea urchins and sand dollars, are classified alongside it in a category called echinoderms, a scientific name meaning spiny skin.

Most species possess five arms radiating from a central disk, although certain varieties develop twenty or more. Remarkably, the animal has neither a brain nor blood. Instead, it circulates seawater through an elaborate network of internal canals, collectively identified as a water vascular system, which accomplishes many of the functions that blood vessels perform in other organisms.

Underneath every arm are hundreds of miniature tube feet. Hydraulic pressure within the canals extends and retracts these appendages, each of which operates like a tiny suction cup. Functioning cooperatively, they enable the echinoderm to adhere securely to rocks and to travel at an extremely gradual pace.

Positioned at the extremity of every arm is a primitive eye spot. Although it is incapable of producing detailed images, it can distinguish illumination from darkness, which helps the animal identify shadows and potential shelter.

Sea stars are formidable predators of clams, mussels, and snails. The hunter envelops a clam with its arms and pulls persistently with its tube feet until the exhausted muscles of its victim permit the shell to separate slightly. It then extends its stomach outward through its mouth and into the narrow opening, where digestion of the soft animal begins immediately.

If a sea star loses an arm to a hungry seabird or crab, it can regenerate a replacement, although this remarkable process may require several months, or occasionally an entire year, to complete.

Twice every day the tide recedes, and during this period of exposure, sea stars shelter in tide pools or underneath damp seaweed until the returning water covers them again. These animals also inhabit the Red Sea along the coastline of Saudi Arabia, where one particular species, the crown-of-thorns sea star, devours living coral. Because sea stars regulate the populations of numerous other animals, they occupy a significant position within their ecosystem. Consequently, visitors who encounter one should observe it attentively while leaving it undisturbed in its natural environment.

questions.why: The article explains how the sea star's water vascular system, tube feet, feeding method, and regeneration help it survive.

wrong.A: The article states that sea stars are not fish.
wrong.B: The crown-of-thorns is one example, and the article makes no such claim.
wrong.D: Tide pools form at low tide; they are the setting, not the main idea.

questions.stem: What does a sea star use in place of blood?
options: A water vascular system
A network of gills
A pair of lungs
A large heart and veins
questions.why: The article says the sea star circulates seawater through internal canals called a water vascular system.

wrong.B: The article says sea stars lack gills.
wrong.D: A sea star has no blood, so it has no blood-pumping heart and veins.

questions.stem: According to the article, why does the clam's shell finally open?
options: The sea star cracks it with its mouth.
The tide washes it open.
The sea star's stomach melts the shell.
The clam's muscles become exhausted.
questions.why: The sea star pulls steadily until the clam's tired, exhausted muscles allow the shell to open slightly.

wrong.A: The article does not say the sea star cracks shells.
wrong.B: The tide is not part of the hunting process.
wrong.C: The stomach digests the soft animal, not the shell.

questions.stem: "It can regenerate a replacement." What does regenerate mean?
options: Remember
Grow again
Throw away
Protect
questions.why: The sentence explains that after losing an arm, the sea star can produce a new one, which means grow again.

wrong.A: The sentence is about a body part, not memory.
wrong.C: The arm is already lost; the sea star does not throw anything away.
wrong.D: Protecting does not create a replacement.

questions.stem: According to the article, why are sea stars important to their ecosystem?
options: They are the main food for every fish in the sea.
They control the populations of other animals.
They clean seawater with their tube feet.
They build coral reefs in the Red Sea.
questions.why: The article says that because sea stars regulate the populations of other animals, they play an important role.

wrong.A: The article does not say sea stars feed every fish.
wrong.C: Tube feet are for gripping and moving, not cleaning water.
wrong.D: One species eats coral; none build reefs.

questions.stem: The eye spot senses light and darkness. What can be inferred from this detail?
options: Sea stars may move toward darker places to find shelter.
Sea stars can read shapes and patterns on nearby rocks.
Sea stars hunt only at night.
Sea stars can see colors clearly.
questions.why: The article says the eye spot helps the animal identify shadows and shelter, so it likely uses darkness to find hiding places.

wrong.B: The article says the eye spot cannot form detailed images.
wrong.C: The article does not say when sea stars hunt.
wrong.D: Nothing in the article suggests color vision.

questions.stem: Why would a sea star be at risk if a visitor kept it out of the water for a long time?
options: It would quickly grow too many new arms.
It would turn into a fish.
It would lose its eye spots.
It depends on seawater moving through its body.
questions.why: A sea star circulates seawater through its water vascular system, so it needs to stay in water to work properly.

wrong.A: Regeneration happens only after an arm is lost.
wrong.B: A sea star cannot become a fish.
wrong.C: The article does not link being out of water to losing eye spots.

questions.stem: Why does the author begin by explaining that a sea star is not a fish?
options: To prove that starfish is the scientific name
To describe how fish hunt clams
To correct a common misunderstanding
To compare sea stars with sharks
questions.why: Many people call it a starfish, so the author first corrects this idea before explaining what a sea star really is.

wrong.A: The author says starfish is a common name that is misleading.
wrong.B: Fish hunting clams is not discussed.

HIGH.prompt: Should visitors be allowed to pick up sea stars in tide pools? Take a position and support it with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
